source.title: Minimizers of the Empirical Risk and Risk Monotonicity
source.authors: M. Loog; T. Viering; A. Mey

record.tranche_reason: The study tests expected risk as training-sample size changes and refines the interpolation-based account: it gives theoretical and experimental cases of nonmonotonicity that it says are not due to peaking or jamming.
record.gate_note: The paper's own results concern sample-size risk monotonicity, not model-size or epoch sweeps. Its references to double descent and jamming are prior work, not results from this study. Figure 1c also examines regularization, but does not test a double-descent peak or optimal regularization.
record.test_reason: The study shows expected risk can rise with more training data, but only where model complexity is small relative to sample size. The authors state this is 'not due to jamming or peaking' (double descent). It does not test V3's claim about behaviour near the interpolation threshold, nor any other version. Double descent and peaking appear only as cited prior work in Section 2.2. The result is recorded under fits_no_version. A T5 reading (V3 should be restated more broadly) is possible, but the paper makes no argument against V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The paraphrase should add two points. First, the authors stress the nonmonotonicity can persist at any sample size. Second, it arises where learner complexity is small relative to n, so it is not explained by peaking/double descent/jamming or by dipping. They also note that regularization does not necessarily fix it, and leave a full characterization open.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies expected risk as training-sample size changes for several ERM learners, with theoretical counterexamples and exact illustrative learning curves. It does not reproduce model-size or epoch-wise double descent.
record.method_sensitivity: The examples vary loss, distribution, intercept, and regularization. In Figure 1c, the unregularized learner is monotonic while the regularized learner is nonmonotonic under the same distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: For standard ERM learners (linear squared, absolute and hinge loss; 1-D normal variance), expected risk in the learner's own loss can increase with one more sample at arbitrarily large n. This is proven for some distributions and shown in exact 1-D curves. It occurs where complexity is small relative to n and is not due to peaking or dipping. Small L2 regularization can create nonmonotonicity where ERM is monotonic.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sample-wise risk nonmonotonicity (more data hurts) can occur far from the interpolation threshold, at any sample size, for simple ERM learners evaluated on their training loss.

record.problems: The experimental evidence is illustrative and primarily reported as plots without numerical curve values or uncertainty estimates. The study does not test whether its sample-size nonmonotonicity occurs near an interpolation threshold.

untested.parts: No learning curves near the interpolation threshold (n≈d). The authors explicitly place their examples away from it.
No noise manipulation, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization. Fig 1c uses only a fixed small λ=0.01/n.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V3 and labelled 'supports'. However, V3 specifies the effect near the interpolation threshold, and the paper explicitly distinguishes its results from that regime ('not due to jamming or peaking'). The V3 link and the supports label are therefore removed. Experiments are 1-D with n≤40 and reported only as figures. Code: github.com/tomviering/RiskMonotonicity. NeurIPS 2019.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or test error curve over model size.
The study tests whether increasing sample size can raise expected risk in constructed ERM settings, but does not test whether the increase occurs near an interpolation threshold.
No capacity sweep across model classes or risk curve past an interpolation point.
No single effective-complexity measure is evaluated across axes.
The paper does not test noise as a cause of a peak, multiple-descent peaks, or optimally tuned regularization's effect on a peak.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective parameter measure.

rows.operation_detail: Theoretical analysis of expected risk as training-sample size increases.
rows.measure: Expected risk monotonicity with training-sample size
rows.note: Positive monotonicity example; the paper states that expected negative log-likelihood decreases as sample size increases.
rows.check: Positive control: the normal-mean learner is provably monotonic. It measures sample-wise risk monotonicity away from any interpolation threshold, not V3's near-threshold effect.

reader_labels.reason: The theoretical examples and several learning curves show nonmonotonic expected risk, including risk increases with more data (R3–R8, R10–R11); the paper does not establish that these occur near an interpolation threshold.
